title: Knights and knaves count
observableEvidence: Tests each possible type assignment against truth-teller and liar rules to force a unique count of knights.
prompt: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. You meet three islanders: P, Q, and R. P says, 'Q is a knight.' Q says, 'P and I are of different types.' R says, 'At least one of P and Q is a knight.' Exactly how many of the three islanders are knights?

contestFormat.eligibility: The MATHCOUNTS Competition Series is open to grades 6-8; a Grade 6 learner is eligible per the official rules.

solutionRepresentation: Suppose P is a knight; then P's claim 'Q is a knight' is true, so Q is a knight. But then Q, a knight, truthfully says P and Q are different types, which contradicts both being knights. So P is a knave. Then P's claim is false, so Q is not a knight, meaning Q is also a knave. Q the knave says P and Q are different types; that statement is false, so P and Q are actually the same type, which fits both being knaves. Now R claims at least one of P and Q is a knight, but both are knaves, so that claim is false; therefore R is a knave. All three are knaves, so the number of knights is 0.
solutionMethod: Assume a type for P, propagate the truth or lie rules through Q and R, and keep the assignment that is fully consistent.

deterministicValidator.equivalenceNotes: Accept the whole number zero in digits or word form, or the word none.

hintSteps.prompt: Test a type for P and use the rule that a knight's statement must be true while a knave's statement must be false.
hintSteps.question: If P were a knight, what would that force Q to be, and does it stay consistent?

hintSteps.prompt: Settle P and Q first from their own statements, then use R's statement about P and Q to fix R's type.
hintSteps.question: After finding P and Q, does R's claim about them come out true or false?

hintSteps.prompt: If a speaker says 'at least one of those two is a knight' but both of those two are liars, then the speaker's claim is false, so the speaker must also be a liar.
hintSteps.question: Once each islander's type is settled, how do you count how many of them are knights?

review.originalityStatement: Original MATHCOUNTS Sprint-style logic problem written from first principles using the classic knights-and-knaves idea; no official MATHCOUNTS problem, wording, or solution is reproduced or paraphrased.

accessibilityNotes: No figure is required; all three statements are stated in text and can be tracked in a written table of possibilities.
accessibleAlternative: Read aloud or display: Knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. P says Q is a knight. Q says P and Q are different types. R says at least one of P and Q is a knight. How many of the three are knights?
